title: First-principles carrier mobility and optical absorption of strained ZnO with self-consistent Hubbard interactions
authors: Hong-Guk Min, Wooil Yang, Sabyasachi Tiwari, Feliciano Giustino, Young-Woo Son
abstract: Carrier mobility and optical absorption are key performance parameters of oxide semiconductors in transparent and flexible displays. We use a newly developed density-functional perturbation theory with a self-consistent Hubbard correction (DFPT+U) to study phonon-limited electron transport and phonon-assisted optical absorption in strained zinc oxide (ZnO). This parameter-free approach accounts for electron-phonon interactions and on-site correlation effects simultaneously. Electronic structures and phonon dispersions are computed under three distinct uniaxial strain directions. Uniaxial tensile strain up to 4.8% along [\bar110] is found to increase the room-temperature electron mobility by 19% while leaving visible-range optical absorption essentially unchanged. These results demonstrate that moderate strain can selectively enhance carrier transport without degrading optical transparency, and establish DFPT+U as an effective framework for predicting strain-dependent transport and optical properties in wide-band-gap oxides with implications for strain-engineered display and optoelectronic applications.
summary: This theoretical study uses an advanced DFPT+U method to examine how strain modifies the electronic and optical properties of ZnO. The research finds that moderate tensile strain can selectively boost electron mobility by 19% without compromising the material's transparency in the visible spectrum. This establishes a powerful computational tool for designing high-performance, strain-engineered oxide semiconductors.
main_problem: The study investigates how strain affects key performance parameters like carrier mobility and optical absorption in oxide semiconductors for use in transparent displays.
main_result: Uniaxial tensile strain up to 4.8% along [\bar{1}10] increases room-temperature electron mobility by 19% while keeping visible-range optical absorption essentially unchanged.
method: The authors employ a newly developed Density-Functional Perturbation Theory with a self-consistent Hubbard correction (DFPT+U) to model electron-phonon interactions and correlation effects.
model_or_system: The system studied is strained Zinc Oxide (ZnO), modeled using first-principles calculations that account for on-site Coulomb repulsion via the Hubbard U term, particularly applied to the O 2p manifold.
key_observables: Room-temperature electron mobility, optical absorption spectrum, lattice parameters ($a', c'$), and band gap energy.
important_parameters: Uniaxial tensile strain ($\varepsilon_{yy}$) up to 4.8%; Hubbard parameter $U_p$; Temperature (300 K).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that the minimal Hubbard correction applied only to the O 2p orbital is sufficient, and it focuses on in-plane tensile strain relevant for thin films.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate atomic structures under strain, electronic/phonon band dispersions, temperature dependence of mobility, and changes in optical absorption spectra as a function of strain.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the theoretical framework (DFPT+U), calculating structural relaxations and electronic properties under varying uniaxial strains, quantifying the resulting changes in carrier transport (mobility) and optical response (absorption).
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state physics, the use of advanced correlated electron methods like DFT+U to model material responses under external perturbations (strain) is relevant for understanding many-body effects in quantum materials.
